strengths: Addresses an important and relatively under-explored problem: safety degradation caused by purely benign instruction fine-tuning, complementing prior work that assumes malicious data in the training set (Qi et al., 2023).

The paper builds its method on an empirical analysis (Module Robustness Analysis via a security-feature proxy) rather than a heuristic alone, and derives three concrete patterns (layer depth, module type Q/K sensitivity, collaborative effects) that motivate the ML-LR design.

Evaluation breadth is strong: five LLMs (Llama2/3, Vicuna), both red-team (AdvBench, Just-Eval) and jailbreak attacks (GCG, PAIR, AutoDAN, SAP30, Comp_Obj), two training scenarios (general-domain and specific-domain), plus usability/expertise assessments.

The authors proactively address a key confound: whether smaller learning rates simply underfit the data. The Fig. 6 experiment (standard IFT at 1 epoch vs. ML-LR at 3 epochs, with training losses reported) meaningfully strengthens the claims, and the all-module LoRA extension (Sec. 6.1) and layer-wise training verification (Fig. 8) support the soundness of the analysis.
Hyperparameters, the search algorithm pseudocode (Alg. 1), and data construction details are provided, giving reasonable, though imperfect, reproducibility.
weaknesses: Validity of the proxy is under-justified. The security classifier is trained on only 100 pairs derived from AdvBench (200 instructions), a benchmark known to contain idiosyncratic/malformed prompts; >97.5% accuracy raises overfitting/leakage concerns, and the paper never validates that proxy performance actually correlates with model harmfulness on held-out attack types before relying on it to steer the search.

Checkpoint selection is potentially unfair and possibly leaky. In the specific-domain scenario, ML-LR gets 2-3 additional epochs and checkpoints are chosen by test-set accuracy; similarly, the general-domain comparison fixes 3 epochs for both methods despite different effective fitting. This weakens the 'no usability cost' claim, and the paper reports single runs with no variance, seeds, or significance testing.

Novelty is moderate: the method is essentially selective layer/module down-weighting, closely related to prior work on safety-critical layers/neurons and freezing-based defenses (e.g., Huang et al. 2024b,c cited in the paper), which is not directly compared against. No baseline mitigation method (e.g., safety regularization, VaccP-style perturbation constraints) is included.

Residual risk remains substantial in several settings (e.g., Table 6 ML-LR ASR of 17.57%, 19.43%, 23.14% vs. base ~4-9%; ASR on #6/#7 still 38-52% for some models), and the perturbation analysis (zeroing half of a weight matrix) may confound module-type findings with parameter-norm effects; the causal story is suggestive rather than established.

Presentation quality is below ACL standards: numerous typos ('Relativley', 'PATTER A', 'gpt-4-1106-previe', 'The numer'), awkward phrasing, radar charts that are hard to read, and overselling language ('pioneering effort'). No code release is mentioned.

strengths: The paper tackles a practically important and under-explored problem: safety degradation of aligned LLMs under benign (non-malicious) instruction fine-tuning, which is more realistic than the widely studied scenario where malicious data is mixed into training data.

The module robustness analysis (Section 3.2) is an interesting empirical probe, and the paper reports clear, consistent patterns (layer depth, module type, collaborative effects) across four/five models, including an appendix analysis on Vicuna.

The evaluation protocol is relatively broad: five open-source LLMs, red-team attacks (AdvBench, Just-Eval) plus five jailbreak attacks (GCG, PAIR, AutoDAN, SAP30, Comp_Obj), two application scenarios (general-domain and a novel private math-domain dataset), and usability/expertise checks alongside security.

The paper anticipates and partially addresses a plausible confound — that a smaller learning rate simply causes under-fitting — via the training-loss-matched comparison in Figure 6/Table 8, and extends LoRA to all modules (Figure 7) to check generality.
Quantitative verification of Pattern A (Figure 8/Table 11), independently training shallow/middle/deep layer bands, supports one of the central empirical claims.
weaknesses: No comparison against any existing defense baseline. Directly related methods that constrain parameter drift during fine-tuning (e.g., Safe LoRA, Vaccine, Booster, Antidote) are cited only in passing or not at all, and none are empirically compared. Without baselines, it is impossible to judge whether ML-LR is a competitive or merely a naive solution (it effectively amounts to freezing most modules via a ~10,000x smaller learning rate).

Potential circularity/contamination between the proxy and the evaluation: the security-feature classifier is trained on 200 AdvBench instructions, and AdvBench is also one of the red-team evaluation sets. Whether the 100 evaluation AdvBench instructions overlap with the proxy's training data is never stated. This could inflate apparent robustness of the identified Mods_Robust.

The link between the analysis and the intervention is weak and potentially inconsistent. Robustness is measured by zeroing weights in the base model's self-attention projections (Algorithm 1 perturbs only self_attn weights), yet ML-LR is applied to LoRA modules including Gate/Down/Up (Figure 11), and the proxy is trained on final-layer hidden representations. A classifier trained on last-layer features plausibly explains why 'shallow layers are sensitive' (Pattern A), which cuts against well-established findings that safety-related features concentrate in middle-to-late layers; the paper does not reconcile this with prior interpretability work.

Fairness of comparisons is questionable: ML-LR checkpoints use 2–3 extra epochs in the specific-domain scenario, and in the general-domain scenario the strategy trains 3 epochs while the under-fitting control gives standard IFT only 1 epoch. Compute-matched comparisons are absent. No random seeds or variance estimates are reported anywhere.

Practicality and cost of the method are under-discussed: the strategy requires training a per-model proxy classifier, a hand-tuned module ranking, and a heuristic search (with a seemingly arbitrary 0.5% threshold in Algorithm 1), plus access to security-related data — resources that a benign-IFT user (the paper's target scenario) would presumably not have.

The magnitude of the mitigation varies a lot across models and attacks (e.g., ASR on #4 GCG remains 42–60% after ML-LR in Table 3; jailbreak defenses on Llama3.1 remain weak), suggesting the method protects against only part of the risk, but this is not analyzed.

Clarity and polish issues undermine confidence: repeated typos ('Relativley Smaller LR', 'PATTER A', 'the numer 9.11', 'gpt-4-1106-previe'), a strange phrase 'inductive fine-tuning (IFT)', the main result for the specific-domain scenario given only as deltas in text rather than clearly in tables, and heavy reliance on radar charts with details deferred to the appendix. No code release or reproducibility statement is provided.

Evaluation relies solely on GPT-4-based judging (GPT-Judge) for harmfulness; no human annotation validation of the judge is reported, which matters because GPT-Judge itself may be sensitive to fine-tuning-induced style changes.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and timely problem: security degradation under entirely benign instruction fine-tuning, a setting less studied than malicious-data-mixing scenarios.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: five LLMs across two model families, two experimental scenarios (general-domain and specific-domain), and seven attack types spanning red-team and jailbreak methods, with both harmfulness scores and attack success rates.

The module robustness analysis yields interpretable findings (depth dependence, Q/K sensitivity, collaborative module effects), and the follow-up training-layer verification (Fig. 8/Table 11) supports Pattern A with actual fine-tuning experiments rather than only perturbation proxies.

Proactively addresses a plausible confound: the checkpoint-selection experiment (Fig. 6/Table 8) controls for the concern that a smaller learning rate simply underfits the data, showing risk mitigation persists at matched or lower training loss.
Reports that usability/expertise is largely preserved (Tables 2-4), which is essential for the method to be practical, and shows the strategy composes with LoRA over all modules (Fig. 7).

Overall the pipeline (proxy construction, analysis, search algorithm, differentiated LRs) is described in enough detail, including pseudo-code and hyperparameters, that a competent lab could attempt replication.
weaknesses: Potential data leakage/circularity in evaluation: the security proxy is trained on 200 Advbench-derived malicious instructions, and the attack evaluation set #1 is drawn from Advbench. The identified Mods_Robust may be partially overfit to Advbench-style prompts, and the proxy's near-perfect accuracy (97.5-100%) likely reflects superficial lexical distinctiveness of Advbench rather than genuine security features. This weakens the causal chain from proxy robustness to real security.

Novelty is moderate: differentiated learning rates across parameter groups/layers is a well-known and fairly direct intervention, and the proxy-guided search embeds hand-crafted heuristics (a fixed module ranking, restriction to the last half of layers, fixed step of 4 layers) that limit the generality and elegance of the method. Claims of being a 'pioneering effort' are overstated.

The perturbation methodology (zeroing half the rows or columns of a weight matrix) is crude; observed sensitivity patterns may partly be artifacts of this specific perturbation scheme rather than intrinsic properties of modules, and no alternative perturbation is tested to confirm.

Evaluation relies on GPT-Judge with an older GPT-4 preview version on relatively small test sets (50-100 samples per attack); no human annotation to validate judge reliability, no multiple seeds, no variance or significance reporting for the headline reductions.

Model diversity is limited: all evaluated models are Llama-derived (Llama2/3, Vicuna), so the claimed patterns and the transferability of Mods_Robust to other architectures (Mistral, Qwen, etc.) remain unverified.

The proxy is trained on the final-position last-layer representation of the base aligned model; whether the proxy remains a valid security measure as fine-tuning progresses (representation drift) is not analyzed, although it is used only pre-training for Mods_Robust identification.

The smaller learning rate (2e-8 vs 2e-4) appears tuned per scenario, and checkpoint selection in the specific-domain scenario favors the method (accuracy-close checkpoint with 2-3 extra epochs); a systematic hyperparameter sensitivity study is missing.

No code or data release is mentioned, and the manuscript contains multiple typos and inconsistencies ('PATTER A', 'Relativley', 'gpt-4-1106-previe', 'numer') that suggest insufficient polish; Algorithm 1 is hard to parse and the hard-coded 'our_ranked' list is not justified quantitatively.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: in-training defenses against safety degradation during instruction fine-tuning, complementing the largely pre-training/post-training defense literature.

The two-stage analysis (verifying security feature space drift via cross-model classifier evaluation, then module-level robustness analysis via pruning-based perturbations) is a reasonable diagnostic framework, and the verification experiments (Table 4, Figure 5, Figures 6-8) provide some support for the hypothesized mechanism.

Empirically broad evaluation: three LLMs (Llama2-7B, Llama3-8B, Qwen2-7B), two IFT datasets, two scenarios (Benign/Attack IFT), and six attack settings spanning red-team and jailbreak methods, with both ASR and GPT-Judge harmfulness scores, plus task performance reporting.
Demonstrates composability: SWAT combined with IFTsafe and Resta/DARE yields larger security gains than any single method, which is a useful practical finding.
Includes an ablation of the Instruction Modeling component (Table 7), pseudo-code for the search algorithm, test-sample examples, and honest Limitations and Ethical Considerations sections.
weaknesses: Potential data contamination undermines security conclusions: Advbench malicious instructions are used to construct the classifier training data (Sec. 3.1) and Advbench also serves as a red-team evaluation benchmark; the relationship between the 110 evaluation instructions and the 100 classifier-training malicious pairs is not clarified, and the classifier itself is trained on only 100 manually built pairs, which is very small.

The robustness analysis and resulting ModsRob search are tied to a specific perturbation scheme (zeroing half the rows/columns of Q/K/V/O LoRA targets) and to LoRA-only fine-tuning; no evidence is given that the findings or the method transfer to full fine-tuning, different LoRA target sets, or finer granularity, limiting generality of the central claims.

Reported improvements are inconsistent and sometimes negative: on Qwen2-7B, SWAT underperforms standard IFT on several attacks (e.g., SAP30 ASR 90.91% vs 89.09%, Avg delta only 36.96%), PAIR remains largely undefended across all methods (52-78% ASR), and the 'w Both' variant completely destroys Llama3-8B's language ability. These failures are not analyzed and temper the claimed breadth of effectiveness.

The causal story ('shifts the learning burden', 'low-level vs high-level features') is largely post-hoc; the update-magnitude analysis (Fig. 5) shows correlation with the design, but no experiment establishes that reduced updates to the non-robust subset are the cause of improved safety rather than a side effect.

Reproducibility and rigor gaps: single runs with no variance, seeds, or significance testing; warm-up epochs are 4 for Llama2 but 16 for the other models with no justification or sensitivity analysis; key experimental details (classifier hyperparameters, search threshold sensitivity) are missing; no code or data release is stated.

Baseline treatment is incomplete: the prior in-training approach (Wei et al., 2024b) that motivates the paper is discussed only textually rather than reproduced, and comparison baselines exclude other relevant safe fine-tuning or data-curation defenses (e.g., Liu et al., 2024).

Presentation issues reduce clarity: multiple typos ('Securty', 'Probelm', 'numer'), dimensionally inconsistent notation (Eq. 1's W2 vs bias vectors, Eq. 3's L2 usage), dense hard-to-read figures (Figs. 3-5), and an appendix where Figure 7/8 captions appear duplicated/mislabeled.

The security feature space drift evidence rests on cross-classifier accuracy drops that could partially reflect general distribution shift rather than a security-specific phenomenon; the claimed security-specificity of the 200-pair dataset is asserted but not validated against confounds.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and relevant problem: safety degradation caused by instruction fine-tuning, and targets the underexplored in-training defense setting rather than pre- or post-training.

Combines an empirical analysis (security feature space drift, module-level robustness via perturbation) with a concrete method (SWAT: warm-up on an identified robust module subset followed by full IFT), giving the method a stated motivating mechanism rather than being purely heuristic.

Reasonably broad evaluation protocol: three LLMs (Llama2-7B, Llama3-8B, Qwen2-7B), two task datasets plus Alpaca mixing, two threat scenarios (benign and attack-mixed IFT), and six attack suites spanning red-team and manual/automated jailbreaks, with baselines including IFT_safe, Safe LoRA, and Resta/DARE.

Includes supporting analyses beyond headline numbers: intermediate state Mwarm performance, parameter update magnitude analysis, verification of the layer-depth pattern, and an ablation of Instruction Modeling during warm-up.
Reports both attack success rate and a GPT-judged harmfulness score, and examines task-performance trade-offs relative to post-training baselines, which often degrade task accuracy more.
weaknesses: Missing the decisive control experiment: a warm-up phase over a randomly selected (or otherwise matched) subset of modules is never compared against warm-up over Mods_Rob. Without this, it is impossible to determine whether the identified robust subset matters at all, or whether any warm-up schedule that lowers early loss produces the same effect. This is a core soundness gap for the paper's central claim.

The claimed causal chain is weakly established. 'Security feature space drift' is measured only via cross-model performance of simple two-layer classifiers trained on 100 manually constructed pairs, and the link between this drift and actual attack susceptibility is asserted rather than demonstrated. The perturbation analysis (zeroing half the rows/columns of attention weights) is a very crude and arguably unrealistic proxy for learning dynamics.

Small evaluation sets throughout: ~110 red-team prompts per benchmark, 100/50 samples per jailbreak method, 100 classifier training pairs, 500 task test samples. No statistical significance testing, no variance over random seeds, and ASR differences of a few points (frequently highlighted as improvements) are well within plausible noise.

Results are fragile and inconsistent across settings: on Qwen2-7B, SWAT fails to help or even hurts on several attacks (e.g., SAP30 ASR 90.91% vs. IFT's 89.09%; PAIR remains high); combining SWAT with both baselines reportedly 'completely destroys' Llama3-8B's language ability. The method's reliability and when it helps are not characterized.

Methodological details are ad hoc and under-justified: magic-number thresholds (acc_base - 0.5%), warm-up epochs of 4 vs. 16 across models without rationale, a heuristic depth-first/breadth search guided by hand-derived patterns, and the approach is tied to LoRA on Q/K/V/O only, limiting generality. Computational cost of the search algorithm is not discussed.

Evaluation metrics are questionable: ASR relies on a rule-based check for 'security expressions,' and HS depends on a GPT-4o judge whose reliability/prompting is not validated. Task performance for UltraInteract/GSM8K is a single accuracy number on 500 samples with no standard instruct-following benchmark (e.g., MT-Bench/AlpacaEval) to assess general capability retention.

Reproducibility concerns: no code or data release is mentioned; the classifier data construction and search procedure would be difficult to replicate exactly; several appendix tables referenced in the text are essential to the claims but the main text omits corresponding detail.

Presentation quality is below bar: repeated typos ('Securty', 'Probelm', 'numer', 'representions', 'perb'), overstatements in Fig. 1 ('tuned LLMs always generate harmful responses'), and unclear figure labeling.

Novelty is moderate: the observation that deeper layers are safer to tune and the general idea of warm-up/staged training are both established; the contribution is largely an application of these observations plus a module search, which weakens the case for main-conference impact even if the experiments were fully convincing.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem — safety degradation caused by instruction fine-tuning — and fills a genuine gap, since most existing defenses are pre- or post-training methods while in-training approaches are underexplored.

The empirical evaluation is relatively broad: three LLMs (Llama2-7B, Llama3-8B, Qwen2-7B), two IFT datasets (UltraInteract, GSM8K), two scenarios (benign and attack IFT), four jailbreak attacks plus red-team benchmarks (Advbench, CatQA), two security metrics (ASR, GPT-Judge HS), and combination with pre-/post-training baselines (IFTsafe, LoRAsafe, Resta).

The paper goes beyond raw results with supporting analyses: performance of the intermediate Mwarm state, parameter update magnitude analysis, and verification of the layer-depth pattern, which strengthens the mechanism story.

The proposed method (warm-up on a searched robust module subset followed by full-parameter IFT) is simple, lightweight, and composable, and Table 1 provides direct evidence that SWAT mitigates the measured feature-space drift.
The limitations section is honest, acknowledging that security feature drift is only one cause of safety risks and that residual risks remain.
weaknesses: The security classifier that anchors the entire analysis is trained on only 100 manually constructed benign/malicious pairs and tested on 100 more. This is very small, and the Advbench-derived data overlaps with the Advbench evaluation set, raising concerns about spurious correlations and about the representativeness of the 'security feature space' — the paper provides no ablation on classifier data size or on confounds like instruction length/style.

No variance reporting at all: no random seeds, no repeated runs, no error bars or statistical significance tests, despite very small security test sets (e.g., 50 samples per automated jailbreak), where a few flipped responses change ASR by several points. Many claimed improvements (e.g., 0.27 HS differences) are within plausible noise.

Generality is limited: all tuning is LoRA on Q/K/V/O only; results may not transfer to full fine-tuning or other module targets. Also, Mwarm training uses different warm-up epoch counts across models (4 vs 16) without justification or sensitivity analysis.

Results are inconsistent across models in ways the paper does not adequately address: Qwen2-7B shows much weaker SWAT gains, PAIR is barely mitigated everywhere (e.g., 62% vs 68% ASR), and Table 5 reports that 'LLM's language ability is completely destroyed' for Llama3-8B w Both — a catastrophic failure noted only in passing in a table cell.

The 'robustness' measure (zeroing row/column halves of weight matrices) is a crude perturbation; the claim that Patterns A/B/C causally explain IFT safety degradation, or that ModsRob robustness is the mechanism of SWAT's benefit, is only correlatorily supported (Fig. 5).

Reproducibility is weakened: no code or data release is mentioned, hyperparameter search details for the classifier-guided search (threshold 0.5%, depth/breadth choices) are thin, and the task performance metric ('500 test samples ... task accuracy') is underspecified for the two datasets.

Several metrics and comparisons are confusing: the Δ column definition relative to IFT is only inferable, Table 1 lacks a Cswat trained/evaluated symmetric entry in some cells, and the writing contains numerous typos and notation inconsistencies ('Securty', 'Probelm', 'numer', Eq. 2 'h^perb', Alg. 1 vs. text mismatches).
